script.opening: "Morning doctor — bit of a fuss over nothing, this. The wife saw a bit of colour in the bowl and won’t let it go. I’ve been having beetroot with my lunches, you see, and these new vitamin tablets. You know how the wives are. Quick once-over and we’ll say no more about it?"

facts.text: Twice in the past week: urine pink-to-red through the WHOLE stream, painless, no clots. Normal colour in between. If pushed on beetroot: "well — it was red-ish… properly red, I suppose, the second time."
Mild slowing of stream for a year or two ("normal at my age"). No burning, no fever, no loin pain, no weight loss. Never had this before.
30 pack-years, quit 5 years ago after a health scare of Stan’s. Forty years as a painter-decorator — solvents and old paints, if occupational history is taken.

Only if his deflection is gently challenged: his best friend Stan died of bladder cancer two years ago — "eighteen months from the first sign to the funeral". The first sign was blood in the water. Vic has thought of nothing else since the second pink bowl.
Revealed late, or when investigations are discussed: golden-wedding anniversary cruise, booked two years, leaves in FIVE weeks. The real question he’s circling: "can all this wait until we’re back?"
"Straight question, doctor — is this what Stan had?" He wants honesty, not soothing. His wife Pam doesn’t know about the second episode.

ice.ideas: Officially: beetroot and the multivitamin. Actually believes neither — he saw the colour.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Stan died of bladder cancer 18 months after seeing blood in his urine. Vic is terrified this is the same thing, and equally terrified that saying it out loud makes it real.
ice.expectations: To be told it can wait until after the cruise. Underneath: to be taken seriously by someone who won’t panic him.

cues: "You know how the wives are" — deflection doing the talking; the appointment exists because HE is frightened.
A flat pause after "did you lose anyone to anything like this?" — Stan, arriving.
"We’ve got this cruise, you see — five weeks" — dropped casually; it’s the real consultation.

checkpoints.text: Pins down true visible haematuria vs beetroot: whole-stream red urine twice, painless, no clots — and does not let the beetroot story stand once the colour is established

Screens the rest: UTI symptoms (none), trauma (none), anticoagulants (none — and knows that even ON anticoagulants, visible haematuria still gets investigated), smoking pack-years and occupational dye/solvent exposure
States the threshold out loud: aged 45+ with unexplained visible haematuria = urgent suspected cancer pathway urology referral under NICE NG12 — made TODAY, not pending results

Arranges same-week MSU (exclude infection without delaying referral), U&E, FBC, BP review, and offers PSA with DRE after counselling (NICE NG12: men with visible haematuria; his slow stream too) — and explains what cystoscopy involves in one calm sentence

Challenges the deflection gently and finds Stan — then answers the real question honestly: same symptom, NOT the same story; most investigated haematuria is not cancer, and early-found bladder cancer is very treatable

Surfaces the cruise and solves it concretely: the suspected cancer pathway aims for a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days (NHS Faster Diagnosis Standard) — the timeline can work WITH the cruise, and going investigated beats going frightened
Handles the secret from Pam: encourages honesty without forcing it — "you’ve carried this alone for a week; that’s long enough"
Safety-nets: clot retention / cannot pass urine / heavy persistent bleeding → A&E today; chase the hospital letter if nothing within a week; named GP follow-up booked either way

worked.txt: "Beetroot’s a fair thought — it catches people out. But you’ve described proper red, through the whole stream, twice. I’d be doing you a disservice if I filed that under vegetables. Let’s do this properly."

"There’s a clear rule I work to: visible blood in the urine, over 45, with no infection to explain it — that gets an urgent referral to the bladder specialists, with the aim of an answer within four weeks. Not because I know something bad is there, but because it’s the one symptom we never sit on."
"Vic — you keep telling me this is the wife’s worry, but you rang, and you counted the days between episodes. Has blood in the water ever meant something to someone you knew?"

"Straight answer, since you asked straight: it’s the same SYMPTOM Stan had — that’s exactly why we move fast. But it is not the same story. Stan’s was found late. Most men I refer with this have no cancer at all, and the ones who do, caught at this stage, usually keep both their bladder and their decades."

"Five weeks gives us room. The aim is for you to be seen and tested within about four weeks, often sooner — so you’d most likely board that ship with an answer instead of a secret. The version of this where you wait until you’re back is the only version I’d genuinely worry about."

"Two things tonight: if you can’t pass water at all, or it’s running heavily red with clots, that’s A&E, not a wait. And if no letter lands within a week — ring me, don’t let it drift. I’m booking myself to call you after the camera test either way."

f.learning: NICE NG12: aged 45+ with unexplained visible haematuria (no UTI, or persisting or recurring after UTI treatment) = suspected cancer pathway urology referral — with PSA and DRE considered in men — made on the day, never deferred for convenience, holidays, or a beetroot story. Anticoagulation never explains haematuria away. The consultation’s real work is the hidden agenda: a friend’s death from the same first symptom, and a cruise he’s scared to lose — the reframe ("investigated beats frightened; the timeline works") is what converts referral into attendance.

knowledge.guideline: NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
knowledge.summary: Unexplained visible haematuria at 45 or over, without a urinary tract infection, meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway urology referral — made on the day, not deferred for a beetroot story, test results or a holiday. Smoking and decorating work add to his risk.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for bladder or renal cancer if aged 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection, or visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful UTI treatment. Aged 60 or over with unexplained non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or a raised white cell count: also refer.

points.h: Recurrent UTI is a different route
points.t: NICE NG12: consider a non-urgent referral for bladder cancer in people aged 60 and over with recurrent or persistent unexplained UTI. Do not confuse this with the urgent visible-haematuria criterion.

Beetroot, some drugs (for example rifampicin) and some foods can colour urine, but whole-stream red urine on two occasions should be treated as haematuria. A urine test for blood and a culture help; neither should delay the referral. Anticoagulants never explain visible haematuria away.
Smoking is the leading modifiable risk factor for bladder cancer; occupational exposure to paints, dyes and solvents adds risk. Take a pack-year and occupational history.

NICE NG12: consider a PSA test and digital rectal examination in men with visible haematuria, and in men with lower urinary tract symptoms. His slow stream is another reason to offer this, with PSA counselling.

Flexible cystoscopy under local anaesthetic, usually with upper-tract imaging such as CT urography; check U&E and eGFR before contrast. The Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral. Most people referred with haematuria do not have cancer.

Characterised whole-stream painless visible haematuria; screened for infection, trauma, anticoagulants, clots and weight loss.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Victor Aldridge? It’s Dr Clarke from the surgery. Could you confirm your date of birth, and are you somewhere you can talk?

Yes, I’m in the garden. Morning, doctor — bit of a fuss over nothing, this. The wife saw a bit of colour in the bowl and won’t let it go. I’ve been having beetroot with my lunches, you see, and these new vitamin tablets. You know how the wives are. Quick once-over and we’ll say no more about it?
I’m glad you rang, Victor. Let me ask a few questions about what you saw, then I’ll tell you honestly what I think and what I’d suggest. Is that alright?
model.why: Sets a clear agenda without accepting the deflection

model.text: Fire away. And it’s Vic.
Tell me exactly what you saw, Vic.
Twice last week. Pinkish. Gone by the next day.
Was the colour through the whole stream, or just at the start or end? Any clots, pain, burning or fever?
model.why: Characterises the haematuria and screens for infection

model.text: Whole stream. No pain at all, no burning, no fever. No clots. (Pause.) Well — it was red-ish. Properly red, I suppose, the second time.
Thank you, that’s important. Any injury, and do you take anything that thins the blood — aspirin, warfarin or similar?
No knocks. Just my blood pressure tablet, ramipril, and the vitamins.
How’s your stream generally, and any weight loss or getting up at night?
Bit slower the last year or two. Normal at my age, isn’t it? No weight loss.
And I see you used to smoke. How much, and what work did you do?
Twenty a day for thirty years; stopped five years back. Painter and decorator, forty years. Paints, thinners, the lot.
Vic, you’ve told me this is your wife’s worry — but you rang, and you remember the colour each time. Has blood in the water ever meant something to someone you knew?
model.why: Challenges the deflection gently and opens the door

model.text: (Flat pause.) My best mate, Stan. Bladder cancer. Eighteen months from the first sign to the funeral. First sign was blood in the water. I’ve thought of nothing else since the second time.
I’m really sorry about Stan. That’s a heavy thing to be carrying — and it explains the last week. Does Pam know how worried you are?
model.why: Acknowledges the fear and explores the secret

model.text: She saw the first one. Not the second. Straight question, doctor — is this what Stan had?

Straight answer, since you asked straight. It’s the same symptom Stan had, and that’s exactly why we move quickly. But it isn’t the same story. Most men I refer with this don’t have cancer at all, and when it is bladder cancer found at this stage, it’s often very treatable.
So what happens?

Beetroot’s a fair thought, but proper red through the whole stream, twice, isn’t something I can put down to vegetables. The rule I follow is simple: visible blood in the urine, over 45, with no infection to explain it, gets an urgent referral to the bladder specialists. I’ll send it today.
model.why: Retires the beetroot story and states the NICE NG12 threshold

model.text: Today? Right.

They’ll usually do a camera test of the bladder — a thin flexible tube, with numbing gel, over in a few minutes, home the same day — and a scan of the kidneys. Before then I’d like a urine sample to check for infection, a blood test for your kidneys and blood count, and a blood pressure check. Because your stream is slower, I’d also like to discuss a prostate blood test and examination — we can talk through the pros and cons when you come in.
model.why: Explains investigations; MSU, U&E and FBC without delaying; PSA per NICE NG12

model.text: The thing is… we’ve got a cruise. Golden wedding. Leaves in five weeks. Can it wait till we’re back?

Congratulations — that’s worth protecting. And five weeks actually works in your favour. The hospital should be in touch within a couple of weeks, and the aim is for an answer within four. You could board that ship knowing, instead of carrying a secret. Waiting until you’re back is the only version I’d genuinely worry about.
model.why: Solves the cruise concretely and turns it into a reason to go

model.text: Knowing. Yes. I’d rather that.

One practical thing — tell your travel insurer about the tests; most want to know about investigations that are under way. And Pam: you’ve carried this on your own for a week. That’s your decision, but it sounds like a heavy thing to hold alone.
model.why: Practical advice and gentle encouragement to share with his wife

model.text: You’re right. I’ll tell her tonight.

If you can’t pass water at all, or it’s running heavily red with clots, that’s A&E the same day — don’t wait for the appointment. If you haven’t heard from the hospital within a week, ring me. And I’ll call you after the camera test, whatever it shows.
model.why: Clot retention and heavy bleeding triggers; chase-the-letter; named follow-up

model.text: Right you are.
So I know I’ve explained it properly — what will you tell Pam tonight?
model.why: Teach-back framed around his real conversation

model.text: That it was proper blood, twice. Urgent referral today — camera test, probably before the cruise. Urine and bloods this week. A&E if I can’t pee or there’s clots. And most of the time it isn’t cancer.
That’s it exactly. Anything else before we finish?
No. Thank you, doctor. I feel lighter, oddly.

social.t: His best friend died of bladder cancer after the same first symptom; he has been frightened alone for a week and has not told his wife about the second episode.
A long-planned anniversary cruise in five weeks is the real question behind the call; solving the timing is what makes him attend.

legal.t: Most travel insurers require declaration of medical conditions and investigations under way; advise him to tell his insurer about the referral before travelling.
Record his forty years as a painter and decorator; occupational history matters clinically and may later be relevant to industrial-injury advice if a cancer were diagnosed.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): be honest and open. GMC Confidential (2017): his information is not shared with his wife without his consent — encourage, don’t force, him to tell her.
Suspected cancer referrals should be tracked by practice systems; document the NICE NG12 criterion, the safety-net and the follow-up call.

community.t: Fight Bladder Cancer and Macmillan Cancer Support for information while waiting; NHS smoking and stop-smoking support remains relevant to his wider health.

playbook.diagnosis: Be straight: “Proper red urine through the whole stream, twice, with no infection, needs urgent investigation at your age. It isn’t a diagnosis of cancer — most men referred don’t have it — but it’s the one symptom we never sit on.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Blood in the urine is like a warning light on the dashboard. Usually it’s something minor, but you don’t drive on for a month to find out — you get it looked at now, while it’s easy to fix.”

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by colluding with the deflection — the beetroot, the wife, the cruise — or by being so alarmed that he disengages. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting beetroot as the explanation, or sending a urine sample and “seeing”.
items.why: Whole-stream red urine twice at 67 meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral; waiting on tests delays it.
items.fix: Establish that it was true blood, state the threshold, and refer today while arranging the MSU and bloods in parallel.

items.fail: Deferring the referral until after the cruise.
items.why: Convenience is not a reason to delay a suspected cancer pathway; the timeline actually fits before he sails.
items.fix: Explain the timescale and make the cruise the reason to go now.

items.fail: Ignoring the slow stream and the occupational history.
items.why: NICE NG12 advises considering PSA and DRE in men with visible haematuria or LUTS; decorating solvents and smoking add bladder risk.
items.fix: Ask about stream and work, record pack-years, and offer a PSA discussion.

items.fail: Treating the call as the wife’s anxiety and never finding Stan.
items.why: The hidden agenda drives his avoidance; unaddressed, he is more likely to delay or miss the appointment.
items.fix: Challenge gently: “You rang, and you remember each time — has blood in the water meant something to someone you knew?”

items.fail: Answering “is this what Stan had?” with “don’t worry, it’s nothing”.
items.why: He asked for honesty; false reassurance loses trust and is clinically untrue at this stage.
items.fix: Answer straight: same symptom, not the same story; most referrals are not cancer; early bladder cancer is often very treatable.

items.fail: No chase instruction or emergency advice.
items.why: Clot retention needs same-day care, and a frightened patient may not chase a missing letter.
items.fix: Name the A&E triggers, the one-week chase rule, and book your own call after the cystoscopy.

timeMap.d: Confirm identity. He minimises (“the wife’s worry”, beetroot) — set an agenda without agreeing it’s nothing.
Whole stream, painless, twice, “properly red”; infection, trauma, anticoagulants; slow stream; pack-years and decorating work.
Gently challenge the deflection and find Stan. Answer “is this what Stan had?” honestly.
Retire the beetroot story; NICE NG12 threshold; referral today; cystoscopy and imaging; MSU, bloods, PSA discussion. Solve the cruise and mention travel insurance.
Clot retention or heavy bleeding — A&E; ring if nothing in a week; call after the camera test; teach-back via what he’ll tell Pam.

wordPics.fail: Accepts the beetroot explanation or defers referral until after the cruise; waits for urine results before referring; never finds Stan; offers bland reassurance; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Establishes true visible haematuria, knows the NICE NG12 threshold and refers on a suspected cancer pathway today, arranges urine and blood tests, explains cystoscopy, and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: challenges the deflection kindly and finds Stan; answers “is this what Stan had?” straight and hopefully; turns the cruise into a reason to be investigated now; discusses PSA; supports him to tell Pam; closes with teach-back and a named call.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably the beetroot — let’s send a urine sample and see.”
avoid.instead: “Proper red through the whole stream, twice, isn’t something I can put down to vegetables — I want you seen urgently.”
avoid.why: Accepting a benign story and waiting on a sample delays a suspected cancer referral.

avoid.dont: “Enjoy your cruise and we’ll sort it out when you’re back.”
avoid.instead: “Five weeks works in your favour — you could board that ship with an answer instead of a secret.”
avoid.why: Deferring the referral for convenience is unsafe management.

avoid.dont: “Try not to worry — it’s almost certainly nothing.”
avoid.instead: “It’s the same symptom Stan had, which is why we move fast — but most men I refer don’t have cancer.”
avoid.why: He asked for honesty; false reassurance loses his trust and the Relating marks.

SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations. Not on anticoagulants or antiplatelets. Retired painter and decorator. Telephone appointment booked this morning: “pink urine last week — wife insisted I ring”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Unexplained visible haematuria at 45 or over, without a urinary tract infection, meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway urology referral — made on the day, not deferred for a beetroot story, test results or a holiday. Smoking and decorating work add to his risk.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for bladder or renal cancer if aged 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection, or visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful UTI treatment. Aged 60 or over with unexplained non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or a raised white cell count: also refer.

points.h: Recurrent UTI is a different route
points.t: NICE NG12: consider a non-urgent referral for bladder cancer in people aged 60 and over with recurrent or persistent unexplained UTI. Do not confuse this with the urgent visible-haematuria criterion.

Beetroot, some drugs (for example rifampicin) and some foods can colour urine, but whole-stream red urine on two occasions should be treated as haematuria. A urine test for blood and a culture help; neither should delay the referral. Anticoagulants never explain visible haematuria away.
Smoking is the leading modifiable risk factor for bladder cancer; occupational exposure to paints, dyes and solvents adds risk. Take a pack-year and occupational history.

NICE NG12: consider a PSA test and digital rectal examination in men with visible haematuria, and in men with lower urinary tract symptoms. His slow stream is another reason to offer this, with PSA counselling.

Flexible cystoscopy under local anaesthetic, usually with upper-tract imaging such as CT urography; check U&E and eGFR before contrast. The Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral. Most people referred with haematuria do not have cancer.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity checked; heard the deflection without accepting it; open question about exactly what he saw.
Retired decorator, married to Pam, golden-wedding cruise in five weeks; Stan’s death.
Heard “you know how the wives are” as armour; the flat pause that brought Stan; the cruise mentioned in passing.
Idea: beetroot and vitamins (not truly believed); concern: the same fate as Stan; expectation: that it can wait until after the cruise.
MSU for culture and urine test for blood, U&E and eGFR, FBC, BP; PSA and DRE discussed (NICE NG12); referral not delayed for results.
Bladder or renal cancer vs UTI, stones, prostate cause or pigment; smoking and occupational exposure recorded.
Characterised whole-stream painless visible haematuria; screened for infection, trauma, anticoagulants, clots and weight loss.
Unexplained painless visible haematuria at 67 in an ex-smoker: suspected urological cancer until investigated.
Suspected cancer pathway urology referral today (NICE NG12); cystoscopy and imaging explained; the cruise timeline addressed.
Slow stream and PSA discussion; BP review; travel-insurance advice; encouraged honesty with Pam.
A&E for clot retention or heavy bleeding; ring if no contact within a week; named GP call after cystoscopy.

social.t: His best friend died of bladder cancer after the same first symptom; he has been frightened alone for a week and has not told his wife about the second episode.
A long-planned anniversary cruise in five weeks is the real question behind the call; solving the timing is what makes him attend.

legal.t: Most travel insurers require declaration of medical conditions and investigations under way; advise him to tell his insurer about the referral before travelling.
Record his forty years as a painter and decorator; occupational history matters clinically and may later be relevant to industrial-injury advice if a cancer were diagnosed.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): be honest and open. GMC Confidential (2017): his information is not shared with his wife without his consent — encourage, don’t force, him to tell her.
Suspected cancer referrals should be tracked by practice systems; document the NICE NG12 criterion, the safety-net and the follow-up call.

community.t: Fight Bladder Cancer and Macmillan Cancer Support for information while waiting; NHS smoking and stop-smoking support remains relevant to his wider health.

redFlags: Painless, whole-stream visible haematuria at 45 or over without UTI — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral
Clots, inability to pass urine or heavy persistent bleeding — same-day A&E
Risk factors: 30 pack-years smoking; forty years’ exposure to paints and solvents; slow stream (prostate)
psychosocial: Retired decorator, married to Pam; golden-wedding cruise in five weeks
Best friend Stan died of bladder cancer 18 months after the first sign
Has not told Pam about the second episode
ice: Idea: beetroot and the new vitamins — officially
Concern: that this is what killed Stan
Expectation: to be told it can wait until after the cruise; underneath, to be taken seriously without panic

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be straight: “Proper red urine through the whole stream, twice, with no infection, needs urgent investigation at your age. It isn’t a diagnosis of cancer — most men referred don’t have it — but it’s the one symptom we never sit on.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Blood in the urine is like a warning light on the dashboard. Usually it’s something minor, but you don’t drive on for a month to find out — you get it looked at now, while it’s easy to fix.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if this is what Stan had. It’s the same symptom — which is why I’m moving fast — but not the same story: his was found late, and yours won’t be.”
management.psychosocial: Make the cruise part of the plan: investigation within the five weeks, travel-insurance advice, and support to share it with Pam.

MSU for culture and a urine test for blood, U&E and eGFR, FBC, BP — without delaying the referral
PSA and DRE discussed with counselling (NICE NG12); explanation of cystoscopy and imaging
safetyNet: Unable to pass urine, clots or heavy persistent bleeding — A&E the same day
Ring if no hospital contact within a week; named GP call after cystoscopy

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by colluding with the deflection — the beetroot, the wife, the cruise — or by being so alarmed that he disengages. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting beetroot as the explanation, or sending a urine sample and “seeing”.
items.why: Whole-stream red urine twice at 67 meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral; waiting on tests delays it.
items.fix: Establish that it was true blood, state the threshold, and refer today while arranging the MSU and bloods in parallel.

items.fail: Deferring the referral until after the cruise.
items.why: Convenience is not a reason to delay a suspected cancer pathway; the timeline actually fits before he sails.
items.fix: Explain the timescale and make the cruise the reason to go now.

items.fail: Ignoring the slow stream and the occupational history.
items.why: NICE NG12 advises considering PSA and DRE in men with visible haematuria or LUTS; decorating solvents and smoking add bladder risk.
items.fix: Ask about stream and work, record pack-years, and offer a PSA discussion.

items.fail: Treating the call as the wife’s anxiety and never finding Stan.
items.why: The hidden agenda drives his avoidance; unaddressed, he is more likely to delay or miss the appointment.
items.fix: Challenge gently: “You rang, and you remember each time — has blood in the water meant something to someone you knew?”

items.fail: Answering “is this what Stan had?” with “don’t worry, it’s nothing”.
items.why: He asked for honesty; false reassurance loses trust and is clinically untrue at this stage.
items.fix: Answer straight: same symptom, not the same story; most referrals are not cancer; early bladder cancer is often very treatable.

items.fail: No chase instruction or emergency advice.
items.why: Clot retention needs same-day care, and a frightened patient may not chase a missing letter.
items.fix: Name the A&E triggers, the one-week chase rule, and book your own call after the cystoscopy.
